Appeal from Original Decree No. 238 of 1991 (Dhaka)
Appeal from Original Decree No. 12 of 1989 (Chittagong)
with
Civil Rule No. 166(F) of 1989
lawyer:
Habibul Islam Bhuiyan with Abul Khaleque, Advocates ----- For the defendant-appellant. 
Nurul Islam Chowdhury with Abul Kalam Azad, Advocates ----- For the Plaintiff-Respondent
parties:
James Finlay PLC ----- Appellant
Vs.
Meshbahuddin Ahmed ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
Md. Mozammel Hoque J: This First Appeal is directed against the judgment and decree passed in Other Suit No. 70 of 1987 by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong, decreeing the suit in favour of the plaintiff. 

 3. Since there was a concluded contract in between the parties, the defendant was bound to execute and register the sale deed. As the defendant refused to execute and register the sale deed, the plaintiff was entitled to a decree. In the plaint the plaintiff made prayer to the effect that a decree be passed for specific performance of contract for sale of the scheduled property to the plaintiff on receipt of the balance consideration with direction to the defendant to execute and register the kabala in favour of the plaintiff on receipt of the balance consideration money within specified time failing which to execute and register the kabala through court on receipt of the balance consideration money. In prayer No. 2 an alternative decree was prayed for to the effect that a sum of Taka 2,15,00,000.00 in favour of the plaintiff against the defendant as compensation and refund of the earnest money with cost of the suit and interest at 20% per annum pendente lite till recovery. 

 4. On receipt of the copy of the plaint the defendant-appellant filed written statement in the court admitting the contract. Further, the defendant informed the court that this suit might be decreed in terms of the prayer of the suit for specific perfor-mance of the contract and balance consideration money should be given to the defendant in accordance with law. After this written statement was filed, the plaintiff filed an application for amendment of the plaint under Order VI rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure making a prayer that prayer-I be deleted. In prayer II the words" in the alternative" be deleted and the prayer II may be amended to the following effect that a decree for Taka 15 lakh be passed against the defendant being the earnest money illegally forfeited with cost of the suit. This amendment in the prayer portion only was allowed. Thereafter the defendant submitted written statement stating that as per terms and conditions of the agreement which are contained both in tender notice and tender form the plaintiff failed to fulfil the term by depositing 25% of the total value of the suit property within the extended time and since the plaintiff failed to fulfil the terms and conditions, the earnest money was forfeited according to the terms as contained in the tender notice itself. 

 5. Both the parties adduced both oral and documentary evidence and after considering the materials on record the learned Subordinate Judge passed a decree in favour of the plaintiff for a sum of Taka 15 lakh i.e. the earnest money which was given to the defendant at the time of submitting the tender. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree the defendant preferred this First Appeal. 

 2. Is the plaintiff entitled to get decree for Taka 15 lakh from the defendant? 

 14. At the very outset Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-appellant, submits that the learned Subordinate Judge committed an error of law and facts in decreeing the suit in favour or the plaintiff. He submits that the learned Subordinate Judge has misconstrued the oral as well as documentary evidence adduced by the parties and as a result an erroneous judgment has been passed in the instant suit. He further submits that the judgment of the trial Court shows that the learned Subordinate Judge had almost accepted all the submissions of the defendant-appellant, but abruptly he passed a decree in favour of the plaintiff decreeing the suit for refund of Taka 15 lakh. Mr. Nurul Islam Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondent, on the other hand, submits that there was no contract at all and since no terms and conditions of the contract had been violated, the defendant was bound to refund the earnest money of Taka 15 lakh. Me. Chowdhury further submits that the term NO.4 as published in the tender notice for sale of the suit property cannot be construed as a term and condition of the contract, and, as such, that condition No. 4 as contained in Exhibit-1 i.e. the paper-advertisement inviting tender, is not binding upon the plaintiff. 

 15. Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan has drawn our attention to the plaint of the suit. It was a suit for specific performance of contract and in the prayer portion there was an alternative prayer for refund of Taka 15 lakh, but main prayer was for a decree for specific performance of contract. Mr. Bhuiyan submits that the defendant filed written statement admitting the grievance of the plaintiff and prayed that a decree might be passed in terms of the prayer in the plaint for a decree for specific performance of contract After the submission of the written statement the plaintiff cleverly filed an application for amendment of the prayer portion of the plaint and prayer No. 1 was deleted and only the prayer for refund of Taka 15 lakh was sought to be amended which was allowed by the court. Mr. Bhuiyan submits that none of the averments made in the plaint had been amended by the plaintiff and in absence of such amendment those averments are still there. Since the plaintiff equivocally made averments in the plaint itself that there was a concluded contract and the defendant was bound by the contract, Mr. Chowdhury, at this appellate stage, cannot retract from the earlier stand taken in the plaint and submit before this court that there was no contract at all. We find substance in the contention of Mr. Bhuiyan. Since the averments in the plaint made by the plaintiff-respondent are still there and have net been amended in any form whatsoever, the plaintiff-respondent cannot run away from the statement of the plaint and it does net leek nice from the mouth of the plaintiff-respondent to say that there is no contract at all. Since the plaintiff admitted that there was a concluded contract and the defendant was bound by the contract, we are .Of the view that there was a contract in between the parties for selling the suit property. 

 20. The learned Subordinate Judge in his judgment has found that the plaintiff did not deposit 25% of the consideration money as per terms of the tender and PW 1 deposed before the court that the terms and conditions to the advertisement of the tender were binding upon him. He further found that clause Nos. 4. 6 and 12 of the draft agreement were sought to be amended by the plaintiff although there was a condition that the terms and conditions of agreement for sale would be settled by the defendant and the tenderer would be bound by those terms and conditions. Mr. Bhuiyan submits that the plaintiff failed to show that any terms and conditions of the draft agreement for sale was unreasonable or absurd which could not be fulfilled by the plaintiff. We have also gone through the draft agreement for sale and we are of the view that there was no absurd or unreasonable condition attached anywhere in the draft agreement Exhibit-F. The learned trial Court further made observation to the effect that the terms and conditions of the tender were binding upon both the parties. In spite of above findings the learned Subordinate Judge illegally failed to put reliance upon the terms and conditions of the tender notice vide newspaper Exhibit-l and wrongly found that the terms and conditions as given in the tender form will be only binding upon the plaintiff and since there is no condition for forfeiture the condition of forfeiture contained in the tender notice is not binding. Such a finding cannot be accepted in view of the evidence we have already discussed above. We have gone through the judgment of the trial Court and we are of the view that the learned Subordinate Judge has totally misconstrued the evidence both oral and documentary on record and illegally passed a decree in favour of the plaintiff. Since there was an agreement in between the parties for the sale of the suit property and since that agreement was enforceable in law and since the term of the agreement for depositing 25% of the total consideration money was violated the defendant legally forfeited the earnest money as given by the tenderer. 

 21. Mr. Bhuiyan further submits that in a case like this conduct of the plaintiff should be considered by the court. He has drawn our attention that though there is a condition that within one month from the date of acceptance of the tender the tenderer must pay the 25% of the total consideration money even then on the prayer of the plaintiff-tenderer the defendant extended the time for 20 days but with a condition that other terms and conditions would remain as it is. He submits that the plaintiff has proposed some unreasonable amendments in the draft agreement which they were not entitled to do. Further at any point of time they did not deposit the 25% of the total consideration money in favour of the defendant. The plaintiff in fact was unwilling to perform his part of the contract though the offer was accepted by the plaintiff. Mr. Bhuiyan has further drawn our attention to the written statement. which they first filed in the suit for specific performance of contract, admitting the claim of the plaintiff and made a prayer before the court for passing a decree as per prayer of the plaintiff. Upon such written statement the plaintiff with malafide motive very cleverly made an amendment to the prayer by making an independent prayer for a decree for refund of Taka 15 lakh only by deleting the prayer for specific performance of contract. This shows that the plaintiff had no bonafide intention to purchase the suit property. We find force in the above contentions of Mr. Bhuiyan. Had the plaintiff any bonafide intention to purchase the suit property, on the submission of the first written statement, he could get a decree for specific performance of contract and get the suit property. Above circumstances clearly show that the plaintiff had malafide intention to frustrate the auction sale just after acceptance of the tender of the plaintiff by the defendant In the facts and circumstances of the case, we are of the view that the learned Subordinate Judge had illegally assessed the evidence on record and passed a decree illegally, which cannot be sustained in law and, as such, the decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge is liable to be setaside. 

 In the result, this appeal is allowed with costs and the judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge are hereby set aside and the suit of the plaintiff is hereby dismissed.
